lead: A truss member is loaded only at its two ends, so its internal force is axial. A frame has at least one member loaded at three or more points or along its length; that member carries bending, and its force direction cannot be guessed. Solve by taking the frame apart: draw each member as a free body, show shared pin forces equal and opposite, and use each body's three equilibrium equations. Machines are frames frozen in one position. Wall brackets, nutcrackers, cycle brakes and scissor lifts are analysed this way.
prereq: You need: equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions, free-body diagrams and two-force and three-force bodies from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A truss member is pin-jointed at both ends and carries nothing between them. Exactly two forces act, so they are equal, opposite and along the line joining the pins. This makes the method of joints fast.

A frame is a pin-jointed structure with at least one member that fails that test: it has a load between its ends, connects to three or more pins, or runs past a pin. Then three or more forces act on it, not along its axis; it carries bending as well as direct force, and its internal force direction cannot be read off geometry.
Machines are frames whose parts move: pliers, a cycle brake, a door closer, an excavator arm. Freeze one position and analyse it as a frame. Ignore friction here; friction starts at 3.4.
Every member that is not two-force needs its own free-body diagram with all loads and pin forces.

items: Count unknowns: an unknown pin reaction gives two components; an unknown two-force member gives one magnitude.
Mark two-force members: pinned at exactly two points with no other load; force along the pin line.
Isolate remaining members with loads, pin reactions and two-force forces.
Pair shared pin forces equal and opposite; never draw the same pin force twice in the same direction.
Write ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 per member; take moments about a pin to remove unknowns there.
Check the whole frame as one free body.

blocks.text: F on B from link = T (C − B) / |C − B|
blocks.where: B and C are pin position vectors in m; |C − B| is link length in m; T is link force in N, positive as tension so the arrow on the joint points towards C.

blocks.text: Choose a pin for moments and a direction for resolution before writing equations.

A member with exactly three forces must have their lines of action meeting at one point, or all parallel. From Unit 2, a three-force body is concurrent. This fixes an unknown reaction direction without algebra and checks a finished solution.

A machine has effort and output load at different points; their ratio is mechanical advantage. Statics gives every pin force — jaw of a nutcracker, brake pad pin. Sizing those pins is strength of materials, but forces come from here. Only equilibrium is used; motion is in Unit 6.

figure.caption: Member AB carries the 12 kN load and the link force at B, so it is not two-force. Link BC is pinned only at B and C, so it is two-force and its force lies along BC.

spec.aria: Horizontal beam AB, 3 m, pinned at A and joined by 5 m two-force link BC to pin C 4 m above A, with 12 kN downward load at B.

examples.question: Horizontal member AB is 3 m long and pinned at A. A two-force link BC, 5 m long, joins B to a fixed pin C that lies 4 m vertically above A. A load of 12 kN acts straight down at B. Find the force in link BC and the reaction at A.
steps: Place A = (0, 0), B = (3, 0) and C = (0, 4), all in m. Check the link length: BC = √(3² + 4²) = 5 m, which matches.
AB is not two-force: reaction at A, the 12 kN load at B and the link force at B act — three forces. A two-force member has forces at exactly two points and nothing else. Take AB as its own free body.
Link BC is two-force. Unit vector from B to C is (−3, 4)/5 = (−0.6, +0.8). Force on B from the link is T(−0.6, 0.8), with T in kN, positive for tension.
Take moments about A for member AB. Only the forces at B have a moment, and the lever arm is 3 m: ΣM_A = 3(0.8T − 12) = 0, so 0.8T = 12 and T = 15 kN.
Positive T means tension: the link pulls B towards C with 15 kN.
ΣFx on AB: A_x − 0.6(15) = 0, so A_x = +9 kN, that is 9 kN to the right.
Reaction at A = 9 kN horizontal to the right, along AB. The three-force rule forces this: the load and link force meet at B, so the reaction at A also passes through B.
examples.answer: The link carries 15 kN in tension. The reaction at A is 9 kN horizontal to the right; its vertical component is zero.
examples.check:
import math
L,h,W=3.0,4.0,12.0
d=math.hypot(-L,h); ux,uy=-L/d,h/d
T=W/uy; Ax=-ux*T; Ay=W-uy*T
print(round(d,3),round(T,3),round(Ax,3),round(Ay,3))

examples.question: Same layout: AB = 3 m, C 4 m above A. Put the 12 kN load at the midpoint of AB. Find the link force and the reaction at A.
steps: BC = 5 m; unit vector B to C = (−0.6, 0.8).
ΣM_A on AB: link moment 3(0.8T), load moment 1.5 × 12. So 2.4T − 18 = 0, giving T = 7.5 kN tension.
ΣFx: A_x − 0.6(7.5) = 0, so A_x = 4.5 kN to the right.
Reaction magnitude = √(4.5² + 6²) = 7.5 kN, angle tan⁻¹(6/4.5) = 53.1° above horizontal.
examples.answer: The link carries 7.5 kN in tension. The reaction at A is 7.5 kN at 53.1° above horizontal to the right (4.5 kN right, 6 kN up).
examples.check:
import math
L,h,W=3.0,4.0,12.0
d=math.hypot(-L,h); ux,uy=-L/d,h/d
T=(W*L/2)/(L*uy); Ax=-ux*T; Ay=W-uy*T
print(round(d,3),round(T,3),round(Ax,3),round(Ay,3),round(math.hypot(Ax,Ay),3))

traps: Calling a member two-force because it looks straight. A load between its ends or a third pin destroys that.
Drawing a shared pin force in the same direction on both members. It is equal and opposite on the two free bodies.

Assuming the reaction at A is vertical. That forces A_x = 0, contradicting ΣFx = 0, so the error shows. In this geometry the true reaction lies along AB, so this example cannot catch an 'along the member' guess.
Putting the link force along the beam. A two-force force follows the link line, not the beam.
Reversing the arrow after a negative T. Keep the tension-positive arrow fixed and read the minus sign at the end.

quiz.q: Define a two-force member and state the direction of its force.
quiz.a: A member with forces at exactly two points and no load between them. For equilibrium the two forces are equal, opposite and collinear, so each acts along the line joining the points.

quiz.q: A straight bar is pinned at both ends and carries a 5 kN load at its midpoint. Why is it not two-force?
quiz.a: Three forces act, not two, so the end forces need not be collinear. They must balance the load and produce a bending moment; the bar carries shear and bending, so reaction directions come from its free-body diagram.

quiz.q: Frame: horizontal AB = 4 m, pinned at A. Link BC joins B to C, 3 m vertically above A. A 12 kN load acts down at the midpoint of AB. Find the link force and the reaction at A.
quiz.a: BC = 5 m; unit B to C = (−0.8, 0.6). ΣM_A: 4(0.6T) − 2 × 12 = 0, so T = 10 kN tension. ΣFx: A_x = 0.8 × 10 = 8 kN right. ΣFy: A_y = 12 − 6 = 6 kN up. Reaction = 10 kN at 36.9° above horizontal.

quiz.q: For that frame, what is the force exerted by the link on pin C?
quiz.a: The link pulls C towards B with 10 kN, along CB.

quiz.q: A machine member carries exactly three forces and is in equilibrium. Explain why their lines of action must pass through one point, and how that helps in drawing a free-body diagram.
quiz.a: If the three lines did not meet at one point, taking moments about the meeting point of any two would leave a moment from the third, so equilibrium would fail. Hence the three are concurrent (or parallel). Knowing two lines fixes the third, so an unknown reaction direction follows without solving equations.

quiz.q: Why is a machine analysed in a fixed position rather than while it moves?
quiz.a: Statics needs zero acceleration. Freezing the machine at one instant makes every part a rigid body in equilibrium, so ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0 give the pin forces. Motion belongs to dynamics, in Unit 6.

quiz.q: In a nutcracker, identify which part is the two-force member and why the handle is not.
quiz.a: The short link joining the two handles is pinned at its two ends with nothing in between, so it is two-force and its force lies along the link. Each handle has the hand force, the jaw force on the nut and the pin or link force — three or more forces — so it needs its own free body.

beyond: Not for the exam. Welded frames are statically indeterminate, so stiffness shares load; that leads to matrix analysis and finite elements. Real machines add friction at pins and sliders, so ideal calculations understate effort. Robotics treats an excavator arm or leg as a chain of links; two-force reasoning identifies pure tension links. Search: method of members, three-force body concurrency, static indeterminacy, four-bar linkage analysis.
